criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly states the scaling normalizes logit variance, derives the variance = d_k / std ~ sqrt(d_k) result from independent unit-variance components, and correctly links large logits -> saturated (peaky, near one-hot) softmax -> vanishing softmax gradients into Q/K. Deduct for the reversed claim (large logits -> uniform), for confusing d_k with d_model or number of heads, or for attributing the effect only to numerical exp() overflow.

Full marks: covers what the factor does, the dimension-dependence (why it matters more as d_k grows), the gradient consequence, AND concrete training symptoms, plus a clear verdict on the proposal. Partial credit if one of these strands (e.g. observable symptoms or the dimension-dependence rebuttal) is missing.

Full marks: rebuts the teammate mechanistically -- shows the term scales with dimension so a lower learning rate cannot substitute, and ties the symptoms causally to softmax saturation rather than asserting 'it helps stability.' Partial credit for a correct conclusion with thin or hand-wavy causal chain.

Full marks: concise, well-organized, uses correct terminology (logits, softmax saturation, Jacobian/gradient, head dimension) and clearly separates mechanism from symptoms from verdict. Deduct for disorganized, vague, or jargon-without-meaning answers.

expected_answer_points: The factor normalizes the variance/magnitude of the attention logits (QK^T) so they stay in a well-behaved range regardless of head dimension

Variance argument: for zero-mean, unit-variance q and k components, the dot product over d_k dimensions has variance d_k, so its scale grows like sqrt(d_k); dividing by sqrt(d_k) restores ~unit variance
Unscaled large logits push softmax into a saturated, near one-hot (peaky) regime, effectively collapsing toward argmax over keys
In the saturated regime the softmax gradient (Jacobian ~ p_i(delta_ij - p_j)) becomes vanishingly small, suppressing gradient flow back to Q and K -> vanishing gradients
The effect worsens as d_k grows, so it is dimension-dependent, not a constant an optimizer or lower learning rate can simply absorb
Concrete symptoms: stalled/very slow training, loss plateau or divergence, attention collapsing to a single token, high sensitivity to init/learning rate
Verdict: keep the sqrt(d_k) scaling (or an equivalent temperature); the micro-optimization is not worth breaking training
common_pitfalls: Claiming the scaling exists only to prevent numerical overflow in exp(), missing the variance-normalization and gradient-flow mechanism
Getting the softmax behavior backwards -- saying large unscaled logits make the distribution more uniform, when they actually make it peaky/near one-hot
Confusing d_k (per-head key dimension) with d_model or the number of heads, so the sqrt(d_k) magnitude argument is wrong
Accepting the teammate's premise that a lower learning rate can absorb it, failing to note the term grows with dimension and shifts the softmax to a low-gradient operating point
Stating a vague 'it improves stability' without connecting saturated softmax to the vanishing softmax Jacobian and suppressed gradients on Q and K
Describing symptoms (loss diverges) without any mechanism, or giving mechanism with no observable training symptoms
reference_answer:
Attention computes weights as softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) over values V. The scaling is not a negligible constant: it normalizes the variance of the logits. If the components of a query q and key k are roughly independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product q.k = sum over d_k terms has mean 0 and variance d_k, so its standard deviation grows like sqrt(d_k). Dividing by sqrt(d_k) rescales the logits back to unit variance, keeping their magnitude roughly independent of the head dimension.

Why it matters as d_k grows: with d_k = 64, unscaled logits have a spread of roughly +/-8 or more, which is far into the saturated region of the softmax. Large logits push softmax toward a near one-hot (peaky) distribution -- effectively an argmax over keys. In that regime the softmax Jacobian, p_i(delta_ij - p_j), collapses toward zero, so gradients flowing back into Q and K nearly vanish.

Expected symptoms if removed: very slow or stalled learning, loss plateauing early or diverging, attention collapsing onto a single token, strong sensitivity to initialization and learning rate, and the problem worsening as d_k (head width) increases. A lower learning rate cannot fix this -- the issue is a saturated, low-gradient operating point, not step size, and the offending term scales with dimension rather than being a constant. Verdict: keep the sqrt(d_k) scaling (or an equivalent temperature); the saved multiply is not worth breaking gradient flow.
